name: Programming Foundations
description: A short, optional start for complete beginners: thinking in steps, the core ideas every language shares, reading errors, debugging, Git and using AI well. Needs review before it goes live.

project_ideas.title: Plan, then build, a class survey tally
project_ideas.brief: Before writing any code, write the steps for a program that counts answers to one class survey question. Then build it one step at a time, committing with Git after each step that works.
done_when: Your written steps came before the code.
It runs without errors and counts each answer.
You made at least three Git commits with clear messages.
You can explain each part to a friend.

topics.title: Breaking a problem down
topics.summary: Turn a big task into small steps you can do one at a time.
topics.why_it_matters: Code is a list of small, exact steps. Most beginners get stuck not on the language, but on not knowing the next step.

resources.title: How to Think Like a Programmer

tips: Write the steps in plain words first, then turn each one into code.
If a step feels hard, it's probably two steps. Split it again.

skill_questions.prompt: You want a program that tells a sari-sari store owner which items are low on stock. What's a good first step?
choices: Write the whole program, then test it
List what goes in (items and counts) and what should come out

quiz_items.prompt: Before writing code, write down what goes ___ and what should come out.
quiz_items.hint: Think of a program as a machine with an input side and an output side.

quiz_items.prompt: Do the ___ step first, run it, then add the next one.
quiz_items.hint: Which step could you test on its own in a minute?

quiz_items.prompt: A big task split into small steps is called problem ___.

topics.title: Variables
topics.summary: Store a value under a name and use it later.
topics.why_it_matters: Programs need to remember things, like a score, a name or a count. A variable is how they remember.

resources.title: Storing the information you need: Variables

tips: Give variables names that say what they hold, like members_count, not x.
A variable holds one value at a time; setting it again replaces the old value.

quiz_items.prompt: In Python, members ___ 12 stores 12 in the variable members.
quiz_items.hint: It's one symbol, the same one maths uses for equals.

quiz_items.prompt: A variable is a ___ that points to a value.
quiz_items.hint: What do you call it in code?

quiz_items.prompt: After price = 10 and then price = 15, price holds ___.
quiz_items.hint: Setting it again replaces the old value.

topics.title: Conditions
topics.summary: Make a program choose what to do with if and else.
topics.why_it_matters: Real programs react: warn when stock is low, greet members by name. Conditions are how code makes decisions.

resources.title: Making decisions in your code: conditionals

tips: == compares, = stores. Mixing them up is the most common bug here.
Read an if out loud: "if stock is less than 5, then..."

quiz_items.prompt: ___ stock < 5:
quiz_items.hint: The word that starts a decision.

quiz_items.prompt: To check if two values are equal, use ___.
The part that runs when the condition is false starts with ___.

topics.title: Loops
topics.summary: Repeat steps without writing them again.
topics.why_it_matters: Counting survey answers or printing every member's name means doing the same thing many times. Loops do it for you.
tips: Before running a loop, say how many times it should repeat and when it stops.
A while loop that never changes its condition runs forever. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

skill_questions.prompt: How many times does this print Hi?

quiz_items.prompt: for name in members___
quiz_items.hint: Python lines that start a block end with this.

quiz_items.prompt: A loop that never stops is an ___ loop.
range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and ___.
quiz_items.hint: The stop number is never included.

topics.title: Functions
topics.summary: Name a set of steps so you can reuse it.
topics.why_it_matters: When the same steps appear in many places, a function lets you write them once and fix them in one place.
tips: A good function does one job, and its name says what that job is.
return hands a value back; print only shows it on screen.

quiz_items.prompt: ___ greet(name):
To send a value back from a function, use ___.
The values you pass into a function are called ___.

topics.title: Reading error messages
topics.summary: Find what an error message says is wrong, and where.
topics.why_it_matters: Error messages look scary, but they usually say exactly what went wrong and on which line.
tips: Read the last line first: it names the error.
Then look at the line number it points to, and the line just above it.

skill_questions.prompt: A Python error ends with: NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. What's the most likely cause?
choices: A typo in a variable name

quiz_items.prompt: In a Python traceback, read the ___ line first.
quiz_items.hint: The error's name is at the end.

quiz_items.prompt: SyntaxError usually means the code isn't written in valid ___.
The traceback tells you the line ___ where it went wrong.

topics.title: Debugging
topics.summary: Find and fix a bug step by step instead of guessing.
topics.why_it_matters: Every programmer writes bugs. What matters is a calm way to find them.
tips: Print the values you're unsure about, right before the line that goes wrong.
Change one thing at a time, then run it again.

skill_questions.prompt: Your loop gives the wrong total. What's a good first move?
choices: Print the total inside the loop to see how it changes
Ask a friend to rewrite it

quiz_items.prompt: A mistake in code that makes it do the wrong thing is called a ___.
Adding print(x) to see what x holds is a simple way to ___.
Change ___ thing at a time, then run it again.

topics.title: Git basics
topics.summary: Save versions of your project so you can go back if something breaks.
topics.why_it_matters: Without versions, one bad change can lose a day's work. Git keeps every saved version of your project.
tips: Commit when something works, with a message that says what changed.
Git keeps history on your computer; GitHub is a website that stores a copy online.

skill_questions.prompt: What does a Git commit do?
choices: Uploads your code to the internet
Saves a version of your project you can go back to

quiz_items.prompt: git ___ -m "Add the stock counter"
Before committing, you choose files with git ___.
quiz_items.hint: You add them to the next commit.

quiz_items.prompt: A website that keeps an online copy of Git projects is ___.

topics.title: Using AI responsibly
topics.summary: Use AI tools to learn faster without letting them do your learning for you.
topics.why_it_matters: AI can explain and hint, but it can also be wrong, and copying its code means you don't learn it. Many classes have rules about it too.

resources.title: Responsible use of GitHub Copilot code completion

tips: Ask AI to explain or hint, then write the code yourself.
Check your class's rules before using AI on graded work, and say when you did.

skill_questions.prompt: An AI gives you code for your assignment. What should you do?
choices: Understand it, follow your class's rules, and write your own version

quiz_items.prompt: AI answers can be ___, so check them against the docs.
Before using AI on graded work, check your class's ___.
Ask AI for a hint, then write the code ___.
